profiles.name: Lise Olsen
profiles.description: Lise Olsen was a nurse and animal rights activist who on July 4, 1992 hung a banner in protest of fur farms over a railroad bridge near her home. The banner was illuminated by homemade lanterns. The FBI claimed the lanterns which were made of peanut butter jars were explosive devices despite bomb experts stating they had no incendiary or explosive capacity. During the trial the judge allows prosecutors to refer to Olsen as a terrorist in front of the jury and police officers without expertise falsely testify the lanterns were weapons. Olsen was convicted and sentenced to 4 years in prison despite the trial judge promising probation. While in prison the FBI attempted to charge Olsen with an incident where a consumer grade smoke grenade used in paintball games was found inside the fur section of a local department store. The smoke grenade was not ignited and fingerprints found on them did not match Olsen. No evidence connected Olsen to the grenades and the FBI falsely claimed the smoke grenade was a bomb. Prosecutors attempted multiple times to bring charges against her related to this incident but the Grand Jury refused to indict. The FBI then claimed to be investigating a murder they said Olsen was involved with despite no murder having occurred as pretext to detain family and friends of Olsen for interviews and fingerprinting. During her parole hearing, those who spoke on her behalf including an elderly civil rights activist were soon questioned by the FBI about their connection to her and fingerprinted. On August 4, 1995 her conviction was overturned and a new trial was ordered after a detective admitted during a deposition that he had lied when he claimed Olsen had told him she manufactured Molotov Cocktails. During the new trial Olsen was acquitted of all felonies involving incendiary devices and attempted arson but convicted on, "Unauthorized Use of a Weapon" for possessing more than three tablespoons of gasoline fuel after the jury was falsely instructed on the meaning of the statute and only told it requires someone possess something that could be used as a weapon rather than requiring they intend to use it as a weapon. Olsen was sentenced to 4 years for this single charge. On December 22, 1998 the Appellate Court of Illinois overturned the second conviction.
profiles.finding: Animals Voice TAVM5-1 and Earth First ef_15_1_1 PDFs identify Chicago nurse activist; portrait extraction pending. Model, investigative journalist and UBC nurse are not verified matches.

profiles.name: Richard Racklin
profiles.description: Richard "Doe" Racklin was an ACT UP/Los Angeles activist who disrupted President George H. W. Bush's address at the 1992 Republican National Convention in Houston. Entering with press credentials, he shouted "What about AIDS?" and threw condoms. He was arrested and held in harsh Harris County jail conditions for several days. The surviving account does not give a precise release date; the action occurred during the convention of August 17 to 20, 1992, probably during Bush's August 20 speech.
profiles.finding: Cambridge ACT UP index and direct-action archive are leads; current TCPA litigant and maintenance-manager profile not independently matched to activist.
profiles.rights: No image selected; original credit and rights verification pending.

profiles.name: Jeff Schuerholz
profiles.description: Jeff Schuerholz (sometimes spelled Scheurholz) was an ACT UP/Los Angeles activist who disrupted a Jerry Falwell event during the 1992 Republican National Convention in Houston. Police dragged him from the event, placed a knee on his neck, and took him to the Harris County jail, where he described being confined in an overcrowded cell under deliberately uncomfortable conditions. His incarceration is confirmed, though the source does not state his individual release date; the Houston protesters were generally held through part or all of the convention (August 17 to 20, 1992).
profiles.finding: Activist Video Archive has joint Jeff Schuerholz/Pete Jimenez interview; open failed internal error. LA Blade2023 corroborates ACT UP pair; video still identification and creator rights pending.

profiles.name: Keith Kjoller
profiles.description:
Keith Kjoller is linked to the same 1992 California action as Peter Lumsdaine, in which activists targeted a defense contractor facility connected to the military application of satellite technology. The protest relied on an intentional breach of security and damage intended to be symbolic but operationally disruptive, with the aim of opposing U.S. war preparations and the expansion of precision-strike capability.

Kjoller was arrested and prosecuted, and he and Lumsdaine resolved the case through guilty pleas that carried custodial sentences. His public profile in activist accounts is tied less to conventional political organizing than to willingness to undertake high-risk, high-penalty direct action that predictably culminates in arrest and imprisonment.
profiles.finding: LA Times1992 identifies Keith Joseph Kjoller with Lumsdaine; Earth First ef_13_1_1 article is archival lead. No verified portrait selected.

profiles.name: Anne Bennis
profiles.description: Anne Bennis was a Philadelphia teacher and member of the Atlantic Life Community. On July 5, 1982 she joined eight other activists in the Trident Nein Plowshares action at the General Dynamics Electric Boat shipyard in Groton, Connecticut. Bennis and four others entered the south storage yard, hammered and poured blood on sonar spheres intended for Trident submarines, and hung a banner opposing the weapons. Police arrested her at the shipyard. A jury convicted the nine participants after a trial in New London Superior Court. On November 9, 1982, the judge gave Bennis a suspended sentence because she had no prior arrest record; unlike five of her co-defendants, she was not ordered to serve a jail term.
profiles.finding: Pax Christi2022 firsthand action account identifies Philadelphia teacher Anne Bennis; no identified portrait verified.

profiles.name: John K. Pruner
profiles.description: John K. Pruner was a U.S. Army intelligence analyst who sought recognition as a conscientious objector during the Gulf War. He left his unit in January 1991 and later surrendered. In October 1991 he was convicted of desertion and sentenced to four months of confinement and a dishonorable discharge.

profiles.name: Jwan Claude Rainey
profiles.description: Jwan Claude Rainey, also reported as Jean-Claude Rainey, was a U.S. Marine who sought conscientious-objector status during the Gulf War. He served six days after an initial court-martial for disobedience. In a separate proceeding in September 1991 he was convicted of desertion and missing movement and sentenced to 14 months of confinement.
